I went from one shop to another, buying what was needed to change his appearance. Once that was done, I headed to Little Britain on my own business. Mr. Jaggers was sitting at his desk, but as soon as he saw me, he rose and stood in front of the fire.

“Now, Pip,” he said, “be careful.”

“I will, sir,” I answered. On the way there I had thought carefully about what to say.

“Don’t say anything that could get you into trouble,” said Mr. Jaggers, “or anyone else. Anyone, you understand. Don’t tell me anything. I don’t want to know anything, and I’m not curious.”

Naturally, I understood that he knew the man had arrived.

“All I want, Mr. Jaggers,” I said, “is to confirm that what I’ve been told is true. I have no hope that it isn’t, but at least I can make certain.”

Mr. Jaggers nodded. “Did you say ‘told’ or ‘informed’?” he asked, tilting his head. Instead of looking at me, he stared at the floor as if listening to it. “‘Told’ suggests a spoken conversation. You can’t have a spoken conversation with a man in New South Wales, you know.”

“Then I’ll say ‘informed,’ Mr. Jaggers.”

“Good.”

“A man named Abel Magwitch has informed me that he is the benefactor whose identity I have not known all this time.”

“He is the man,” Mr. Jaggers said, “in New South Wales.”

“And no one else?” I asked.

“No one else,” said Mr. Jaggers.

“I’m not unreasonable enough to blame you for my mistakes and false conclusions, sir. But I always thought it was Miss Havisham.”

“As you say, Pip,” Mr. Jaggers replied, looking at me coolly and biting his forefinger, “I am not responsible for that.”

“But it seemed so much like her, sir,” I pleaded miserably.

“Without a shred of evidence, Pip,” said Mr. Jaggers, shaking his head and gathering his coat tails. “Never trust appearances. Judge everything by the evidence. There is no better rule.”

After standing silently for a moment, I sighed. “I have nothing more to say. I’ve confirmed my information, and that is all.”

“And now that Magwitch—in New South Wales—has finally revealed himself,” Mr. Jaggers said, “you will understand how strictly I have kept to the facts in every conversation with you. I have never departed from the facts in the slightest. You understand that?”

“Completely, sir.”

“When Magwitch—in New South Wales—first wrote to me—from New South Wales—I warned him that he must never expect me to depart from the facts.”

Summer drew onward, and plague, crowned by the sun’s mighty beams, sent her unfailing arrows across the earth. Beneath their power the nations bent their heads and perished. The grain that had risen abundantly lay rotting upon the soil in autumn, while the sorrowful creature who had ventured forth to find bread for his children lay rigid in the furrow, struck down by plague. The green forests swayed their branches in majesty, and beneath their shade the dying lay scattered, replying to that solemn music with discordant cries. Brightly coloured birds darted through the shadows; untroubled deer rested safely on the fern. Oxen and horses wandered out of unattended stables to graze among the wheat, for death descended upon mankind alone.

Our terror increased with the summer and its deaths. My poor beloved and I gazed at one another, and at our children. “We shall preserve them, Idris,” I said; “I shall save them. In years to come we shall tell them of these fears, vanished then with the cause that brought them. Even should they alone remain upon the earth, they shall yet live; their faces shall not pale, nor their dear voices weaken.” Our eldest understood something of the events surrounding him, and would sometimes question me gravely about the cause of such immense devastation. Yet he was only ten, and youth’s gladness soon drove untimely anxiety from his face. Evelyn, a merry cherub, a playful infant knowing neither suffering nor grief, shook his fair curls from his eyes and filled the halls with echoes of laughter, drawing our notice to his games in a thousand innocent ways. Clara, our sweet and gentle Clara, sustained, consoled, and delighted us. She undertook to nurse the sick, comfort the grieving, help the old, and share the amusements and stir the happiness of the young. Through the rooms she passed like a benevolent spirit sent from heaven to brighten our darkened hour with an unearthly radiance. Thanks and blessings followed her steps. Yet when she stood modestly before us, playing with our little ones or attentively performing small kindnesses for Idris, one wondered in which lovely feature of her innocent beauty, or which tender note of her affecting voice, such courage, wisdom, and untiring goodness could dwell.

Summer dragged slowly by, for we believed winter would at least restrain the illness. Complete deliverance was a hope too precious, too deeply felt, to speak aloud. If anyone carelessly voiced it, the listeners’ streaming tears and impassioned sobs revealed the depth of their dread and the faintness of their hope.

When dinner was over, all the boys went hunting for turtle eggs on the sandbar. They tested the ground with sticks. Wherever the sand felt soft, they dropped to their knees and scooped it away with their hands. Sometimes one hole held fifty or sixty eggs, perfectly round and white and slightly smaller than an English walnut. They had a splendid meal of fried eggs that night, and another on Friday morning.

After breakfast they ran onto the bar, shouting and leaping. They chased each other round and round, throwing off clothes as they went until they wore nothing. Then they took their games far up the sandbar through the shallow water. The current was strong, and every so often it knocked their feet away, which only made everything funnier. Sometimes they crouched together and splashed water into each other’s faces with their hands. They crept nearer, turning their heads aside to avoid choking on the spray. Finally they grabbed one another and wrestled until the strongest pushed another boy under. Then they all tumbled beneath the water in a tangle of white arms and legs, coming up blowing, spluttering, laughing, and trying to catch their breath all at once.

When they could play no longer, they ran out and sprawled on the warm, dry sand. They lay there and piled it over themselves, until they were ready to rush into the water and start the whole game again. At last they noticed that their bare skin looked quite like flesh-coloured circus tights. So they marked a ring in the sand and staged a circus. It had three clowns, since each boy insisted on having that best of all parts.

Afterward they brought out their marbles and played knucks, ringtaw, and keeps until they grew bored. Joe and Huck then returned to the water, but Tom would not risk another swim. When he had kicked his trousers off, he had also lost the string of rattlesnake rattles tied around his ankle. He wondered how he had avoided cramp for so long without the charm’s mysterious protection. He stayed out until he found it. By then the others were tired and ready to stop. Little by little they wandered away from each other, became unhappy, and stared across the wide river with longing at the village sleeping in the sunshine. Tom realized he was writing “BECKY” with his big toe in the sand. Annoyed at his weakness, he rubbed it out. But he could not stop himself from writing it again. He erased the name once more, then kept himself from temptation by gathering the other two boys together and staying with them.
